newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, rebels reopen debate on Chechnya's future.
newsitem.headline: Russia, rebels reopen debate on Chechnya's future.

text.p: Moscow and Chechen separatist rebels on Sunday reopened the debate on the future political status of Russia's breakaway southern region, despite an earlier decision to put off the painful issue by five years.
A senior government official said meanwhile that some countries had been warned Russia could break diplomatic ties with them if they treated Chechnya as an independent state.

Sergei Stepashin, the head of the administrative department, said Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had issued the warning to countries including the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, where support for Chechen separatists is strong.

"Primakov told several ambassadors in Moscow that if their countries hold separate talks or recognise Chechnya's independence, Russia can raise a question of severing diplomatic links with these countries," Stepashin told NTV television.
Stepashin said President Boris Yeltsin had ruled out granting full independence to Chechnya in his fresh guidelines for peace talks with Chechen rebels.
"Russia's territorial integrity cannot be a subject of trade," he quoted Yeltsin's instructions to the Russian negotiating team as saying.
On August 31 rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov and Russian security chief Alexander Lebed signed a peace deal which ended 21 months of war.
Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, have died in the conflict launched in December 1994, when Russia sent troops to quell the southern region's independence bid.

Under the deal Russian troops, who have failed to establish control over most of Chechnya, started withdrawing from the region. The rebels agreed to put off for five years a decision on whether Chechnya would become independent.

President Boris Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, last Thursday backed Lebed, saying in a radio address that the former paratroop general had carried out his instructions to promptly end the war.
But the two sides appeared to have conflicting interpretations of the deal.

Lebed has said he was certain it improved the chances of keeping Chechnya part of Russia. Five years of peace and the realities of life in landlocked Chechnya would make separatists more willing to reduce their demands to ones for strong autonomy, he said.
His opponents attacked him in parliament last week, saying that the agreement in fact rubber-stamped Chechnya's secession.
Many deputies in the lower house loudly cheered Lebed's opponent, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, when he branded the deal a "humiliating admission of defeat".
Maskhadov, confirming the suspicions of opponents of the agreement, declared in a television interview shown on Sunday that Chechnya would never agree to be part of Russia.

"No Chechen has ever signed any kind of document saying that Chechnya is a part of Russia and there will never be such a Chechen," Maskhadov told Russian Public Television, adding however that the region could maintain close ties with Russia.
Interfax news agency later quoted an unnamed senior government official as saying that Maskhadov's statement had "seriously complicated the process of peaceful settlement of the conflict".

In a clear indication of a toughening Russian position, Stepashin said Yeltsin had demanded a stronger role for Moscow in forming a Chechen coalition government and insisted that some Russian troops remain on Chechen territory, as had been agreed in earlier agreements with the rebels.
